title: Coffee Ratings
text:
Introduction This analysis explores the Coffee Ratings dataset from TidyTuesday. The Coffee Ratings dataset contains reviews and scores of different coffees from around the world.
Data Sources: - TidyTuesday Coffee Ratings - Original Data: Coffee Quality Institute (CQI) via James LeDoux.
Analysis


Code
library(tidyverse)

# Load data
coffee_ratings <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2020/2020-07-07/coffee_ratings.csv')

# find the top countries by counting them
coffee_counts <- coffee_ratings |> 
  group_by(country_of_origin) |> 
  summarize(total = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(total)) |> 
  head(10)

ggplot(data = coffee_counts, aes(x = country_of_origin, y = total)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(
    title = "Where do the most coffee ratings come from?",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Number of Ratings"
  )

title: Lego Sets over Time
text:
Introduction This analysis explores Lego sets over the years to see how the number of sets produced has grown over time.
Data Sources: - TidyTuesday Lego Sets - Original Data: Rebrickable
Analysis


Code
library(tidyverse)

# Load data
lego_sets <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2022/2022-09-06/sets.csv.gz')

# count sets per year
sets_per_year <- lego_sets |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(total_sets = n())

ggplot(data = sets_per_year, aes(x = year, y = total_sets)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Lego Sets over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Sets"
  )

title: How Common Are Primes?
text:
Introduction
This simulation plans to tackle some of the mysterious properties of prime numbers. The main question that drives this analysis is: If you pick a random positive integer near N, how likely is it that it is prime, and how does that change with N? Proved in 1896, the Prime Number Theorem states that the probability is about 1/ln(N). A simulation can be helpful for checking these values, because as N grows, it becomes difficult to calculate whether every number is prime. Instead, we can take a random sample of the numbers between N and 2N, test those for primality, and compare that result to 1/ln(N).
Simulation
The two functions that I wrote are is_prime, and prop_prime. is_prime takes an integer, and if it’s prime returns TRUE, otherwise returns FALSE. prop_prime takes an integer N, and then randomly picks 1,000 integers between N and 2N, each number being equally likely, then returns the proportion of prime numbers chosen.
I mapped these functions because for all the randomly selected 1,000 integers, we want to test if they are prime, so we can use map_lgl on a vector of all of these integers to get a vector that tells us which of the integers are prime. Putting is_prime and prop_prime together, I used map_dbl to repeat this estimate for many values of N, (10^2 through 10^12). This can help us see how the probability changes as N increases.


Code
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(47) # same random numbers every time the page renders

# TRUE if n is prime, FALSE if n is composite. This algorithm just checks
# if any number up to sqrt(n) is a divisor. 
is_prime <- function(n) {
  if (n < 2) return(FALSE)       # 0 and 1 are not prime
  d <- 2
  while (d * d <= n) {           # only need to check divisors up to sqrt(n)
    if (n %% d == 0) return(FALSE) # found a divisor, so n is not prime
    d <- d + 1
  }
  TRUE                           # no divisor found, so n is prime
}

# pick n_samples random integers between N and 2N
# Then, returns the proportion that are prime
prop_prime <- function(N, n_samples = 1000) {
  samples <- N + sample.int(N, n_samples, replace = TRUE) - 1
  mean(map_lgl(samples, is_prime))
}

# This just runs the simulation for N = 10^2, 10^3, ..., 10^12
prime_sims <- tibble(N = 10^(2:12)) |>
  mutate(estimate = map_dbl(N, prop_prime))


Results
On our plot, the dots are our simulated estimates of the likelihood of a number being prime around N, while the line is the function 1/ln(N). Note that the x-axis is on a logarithmic scale. According to the simulated data and our function, the share of primes falls steadily as N increases, going from about 20% near N=100 to about 4% near N= 1 trillion.
Inspecting the graph, the dots stay close to the curve at every tested size for N. The dots do not lay exactly on the line, because each dot comes from only 1,000 random numbers, so randomness is expected. Also, the formula is not meant to be exact, rather an estimate.


Code
ggplot(prime_sims, aes(x = N)) +
  geom_function(fun = \(x) 1 / log(x), aes(color = "Prime Number Theorem: 1/ln(N)")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = estimate, color = "Simulation estimate"), size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Primes around N get rarer as N increases",
    subtitle = "1,000 random integers sampled between N and 2N for each N",
    x = "N (log scale)",
    y = "Proportion that are prime",
    color = NULL
  )









Conclusion
So in conclusion, I wrote a function that tests primality, then estimated the proportion of primes around 11 different values of N by sampling and simulating, and then I compared my estimates to 1/ln(N). My simulation agrees with the Prime Number Theorem. Primes become rarer as N grows, but slowly, and at a predictable rate. In the future, I could make this simulation more accurate by drawing more samples. This would make my estimations less noisy.

title: Satoshi Nakamoto Text Analysis
text:
Introduction This analysis explores the text that Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin, left behind on forums and through emails.
Data Sources: This dataset contains a collection of messages attributed to Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin. Sourced from Bitcoin Forum. This dataset provides insights into the thoughts, technical discussions, and philosophies of one of the most enigmatic figures in modern finance and cryptography. - Kaggle Dataset via Leandro Wrzecionek - Original source: Satoshi Nakamoto’s posts on the Bitcoin Forum (BitcoinTalk), archived by the Satoshi Nakamoto Institute
Analysis


Code
library(tidyverse)

satoshi <- read_csv("data/satoshi_messages.csv") #load the data

#clean the data
satoshi_clean <- satoshi |>
  filter(!is.na(Message)) |>
  mutate(Message = str_replace_all(Message, "\u00a0", " "), #this dataset contains NO-BREAK SPACES, so I replaced them with normal spaces to make it easier down the road
         has_quote = str_detect(Message, "Quote from:")) #creates a new column, has_quote, marking whether the message was a reply to someone else's post

#isolate for replies
quotes <- satoshi_clean |>
  filter(has_quote) |> # keep only the messages where Satoshi quotes someone
  mutate(header = str_extract(Message, "Quote from: .+"), # pull out the first "Quote from: ..." line in each message, .+ stops at the end of a line
         date = mdy(str_extract(header, "[A-Z][a-z]+ \\d{1,2}, \\d{4}")), # find the date (capitalized month, 1–2 digit day, comma, 4-digit year)
         user = str_extract(header, "(?<=Quote from: ).+(?= \\w+ [A-Z][a-z]+ \\d{1,2}, \\d{4})")) |> # lookbehind (?<=Quote from: ): start right after "Quote from: ", .+ will pull the characters that make up the username
            # lookahead (?= \\w+ [A-Z][a-z]+ \\d{1,2}, \\d{4}): stop just before WORD MONTH DAY YEAR. This is becaue the format for the forum replies goes: Quote from: USERNAME on DATE. 
        #So thus, we have extracted the username that Satoshi is replying to
  filter(!is.na(date)) #exclude one case where there is no date


Who Did Satoshi Reply To?
This plot shows a bar for each user that Satoshi replied to at least 4 times, sorted from most replies to fewest replies. Everyone under 4 replies got grouped into “other”.
knightmb (11), gavinandresen (9), jgarzik (8) and theymos (7) got the most replies. Gavin Andresen later became Bitcoin’s lead developer, and Jeff Garzik (jgarzik) became a core developer. Satoshi himself appears 4 times, because he sometimes quoted his own earlier posts. Other is by far the largest bar, with 80 replies spread across 64 users. This means Satoshi responded to a wide community rather than a few insiders.
Limitation: Only the first person quoted in each reply gets counted.


Code
#now lets plot the number of replies per user
quotes |>
  # keep users with 4+ replies; lump everyone else into "Other"
  mutate(user = fct_lump_min(user, min = 4),
         # order the users from most to fewest replies
         user = fct_infreq(user),
         # move "Other" to the end so it doesn't sit with the top users
         user = fct_relevel(user, "Other", after = Inf)) |> 
  # fct_rev() flips the order so the most-replied-to user is at the top
  ggplot(aes(y = fct_rev(user))) +
  # geom_bar() counts the rows (replies) for each user
  geom_bar(fill = "#F7931A") + #bitcoin orange
  labs(title = "Who Satoshi Replied To Most Often on the Forum",
       subtitle = "First user quoted in each reply; users with fewer than 4 replies grouped as \"Other\"",
       x = "Number of replies", y = "Forum username")









When Was Satoshi Most Active?
This plot shows the number of replies per month, from December ’09 to December ’10. The peak is July (31) and August 2010 (42). March–April 2010 has no replies, and the data stops in December 2010.
This peak lines up with Bitcoin’s first big wave of public attention, following a Slashdot article posted July 2010. December 2010 is when Satoshi made his last forum post.
Limitation: the dates belong to the posts Satoshi replied to, not the reply itself.


Code
#now, lets plot the replies over time, by month
quotes |>
  # round each date down to the first day of its month
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  # count how many replies fall in each month
  count(month) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n)) +
  # geom_col() uses the counts we already calculated as bar heights
  geom_col(fill = "#F7931A") +
  # label the x-axis every 2 months as "Mon YYYY"
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "2 months") +
  labs(title = "When Were the Posts Satoshi Replied To Written?",
       subtitle = "Based on the date of the first quoted post in each reply",
       x = "Month", y = "Number of replies")
